text:
Maya: Quick summary — I spun up a small 'z-node' fallback GPU pool via a second Karpenter provisioner to reduce AZ-wide evictions during spot churn. Seeing odd node selection where pods keep landing in the wrong AZ then getting evicted. Anybody seen this pattern?

Jon: Which k8s affinity/taint config did you use? can you paste the provisioner yaml?

Maya: pasted below. it's tiny, basically a provisioner scoped to `us-west-2a` and `us-west-2b` with a separate fallback that allows cross-az. trying to avoid single-AZ hot spots.

Maya: ```yaml
apiVersion: karpenter.sh/v1alpha5
kind: Provisioner
metadata:
  name: gpu-fallback-provisioner
spec:
  ttlSecondsAfterEmpty: 300
  provider:
    subnetSelector:
      karpenter.sh/discovery: us-west-2
    securityGroupSelector:
      kubernetes.io/cluster/redwood: owned
  requirements:
  - key: kubernetes.io/arch
    operator: In
    values: ["amd64"]
  - key: karpenter.sh/capacity-type
    operator: In
    values: ["spot","on-demand"]
  limits:
    resources:
      cpu: 512
      memory: 1Ti
  labels:
    redwood/role: gpu-fallback
  ttlSecondsUntilExpired: 86400
```

Vikram: Thanks. A couple quick checks: 1) Are there multiple provisioners with overlapping selectors? 2) What does the scheduler's NodeAffinity look like for the GPU pods? If they're soft preferred, they can bounce between AZs.

Maya: There are two provisioners: `gpu-primary` (AZ pinned to us-west-2a) and this `gpu-fallback`. Primary has `node.kubernetes.io/zone=us-west-2a` requirement. Pods request `topology.kubernetes.io/zone` via preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution (we use soft preferences in the helm chart).

Kevin: That combination explains some churn — preferredDuringScheduling is not a hard constraint, so kube-scheduler may place a pod on fallback nodes in another AZ when capacity is low, then if primary becomes available and a controller or pod disruption causes reschedule, you'll see evictions.

Lea: Also check AWS ENI limits per AZ on the instance types used. If fallback creates a mix of instance sizes, ENI exhaustion in an AZ can cause surprising placement failures.

Maya: hmm we saw ENI warns earlier, logs pasted: 

Maya: ```
I0323 09:12:04.123456 1 scale.go:231] scale-up: launching 1 node(s) for pods: [training-job-xyz]
E0323 09:12:05.987654 1 awsclient.go:418] AllocateENI: failed: AddressLimitExceeded: The maximum number of ENIs has been reached for subnet subnet-abc123

status code: 400, request id: 111-222
```

Jon: That AddressLimitExceeded is classic: the provisioner might be creating lots of small instances and hitting IP/ENI caps. Two mitigations: 1) switch to instance types with higher ENI densities; 2) consolidate by using fewer larger instances for GPU workloads (reduce per-node overhead).

Maya: Right. We're trying consolidation to cut costs, but worried about cold-start latency for large instances during scale-ups. Any data on tradeoff?

Vikram: From our experiments last quarter: larger GPU instances (8x A10g-style) gave ~30% lower network/ENI overhead and ~10-20% lower per-token serving cost once KV cache warms. Cold-start tail latency increased ~200-400ms on first shard. If your latency SLO tolerates that, consolidation wins for cost.

Kevin: Another angle — set up graceful fallback routing: prefer primary provisioner via pod affinity, but allow fallback only for preflight/batch jobs. For strict low-latency inference routes, force hard zone affinity and provision reserved capacity (Dedicated) or on-demand in the pinned AZ.

Lea: Also watch for drift between provisioner node templates and actual node labels. We had a migration bug where AMI label changed and karpenter didn't reconcile because the provisioner selector was too strict, leading to nodes being orphaned in the wrong pool. Add a periodic audit job that compares provisioner requirements -> actual nodes.

Maya: Good call. We observed orphaned GPU nodes flagged with `karpenter.sh/provisioner=` but not matching the expected instance profile. I'll add an audit query.

Maya: Proposed immediate action items:
- Disable soft zone preference on inference pods (make it required) for the next 24h to stabilize traffic.
- Change fallback provisioner to prefer instance types with higher ENI density (migrate from g4dn.x -> p4d? maybe p4 or g5)
- Add audit job to detect label drift and auto-tag nodes for reclamation
- Run cost sim for consolidation (estimate spot vs on-demand mix)

Jon: Agree. For the audit job, we have a small script I can drop in. It queries `kubectl get nodes -l karpenter.sh/provisioner -o jsonpath` and compares to provisioner requirements in the cluster. Want me to paste?

Maya: please, that'd help.

Jon: ```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# quick drift check
PROVISIONERS=$(kubectl get provisioners -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}\n{end}')
for p in $PROVISIONERS; do
  echo "checking $p"
  reqs=$(kubectl get provisioner $p -o jsonpath='{.spec.requirements}')
  nodes=$(kubectl get nodes -l karpenter.sh/provisioner=$p -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name} {end}')
  echo "reqs: $reqs"
  echo "nodes: $nodes"
  done
```

Vikram: Nice. For long term we should standardize provisioner naming and limit overlap — single-provisioner-per-workload-pattern reduces surprises. Also document the fallback behavior in the runbook.

Lea: Can OpsBot add an alert for ENI saturation per-subnet? We missed the spike earlier.

OpsBot: Added alert 'aws.subnet.eni_exhaustion' threshold=80% -> paging to #eng-oncall. Created runbook link: https://intra.redwood/ops/eni-exhaustion

Maya: Thanks all — I'll implement the required zone affinity for inference, update the fallback instance types, and run the cost sim. I'll post results in ~6 hours. :thumbsup:

Kevin: Ping if you want help running the sim or validating the consolidated perf numbers.

Maya: Will do.
